method: Read primary article/activity narratives and relevant methods, results, procedures, and rights statements. Followed linked source files and legitimate institutional copies where available. Locator searches assisted navigation, not judgments. Selected layout-dependent PDF evidence was visually inspected. No participant-level reanalysis, code execution of source workflows, or blanket validation of linked third-party materials.
limits: Full primary text means a usable source narrative was available, not that every supplement, third-party reference, slide, or software interface was verified.

updates.before: Preservice and in-service special educators and related-service providers each write IEP goals for two written student scenarios that give a student's age, grade, disability identification, likes and dislikes, and assessment scores. For one scenario they write the goal unaided; for the other they fill in a structured template (student name, age, primary disability, goal area, present level, condition, behavior, criterion and time frame), paste it with a one-line instruction into a free chatbot, and copy the generated goal back, with the order of the two conditions randomized. Participants then rate each goal on six items of the Revised IEP/IFSP Goals and Objectives Rating Instrument, which ask whether the target behavior is observable, measurable, functional, generalizable and teachable across daily activities and team members. The researchers also scored the goals against SMART criteria and found that expert raters scored much lower than participants or the chatbot, with formulaic goals earning rubric points an expert would withhold. Participants also wrote how they would use such tools, and many stressed review, individualization and privacy. The products are two goals per participant with their rubric self-ratings and a short written reflection.
updates.after: Preservice and in-service special educators and related-service providers each write IEP goals for two written student scenarios that give a student's age, grade, disability identification, likes and dislikes, and assessment scores. For one scenario they write the goal unaided; for the other they fill in a structured template (student name, age, primary disability, goal area, present level, condition, behavior, criterion and time frame), paste it with a one-line instruction into a free chatbot, and copy the generated goal back, with the order of the two conditions randomized. Participants then rate each goal on six items of the Revised IEP/IFSP Goals and Objectives Rating Instrument, which ask whether the target behavior is observable, measurable, functional, generalizable and teachable across daily activities and team members. The research team scored the goals with R-GORI, and ChatGPT also scored them against SMART criteria. Expert R-GORI ratings tended to be lower than participant and chatbot ratings; the authors note that formulaic goals can earn rubric points that expert judgment would withhold. Participants also wrote how they would use such tools, and many stressed review, individualization and privacy. The products are two goals per participant with their rubric self-ratings and a short written reflection.

updates.before: Mixed-methods replication with 111 participants across four universities (counterbalanced conditions; self, expert and chatbot ratings; open responses); small condition effect that was not significant in mixed-effects models.

The initial mixed model of participant R-GORI self-ratings found no significant condition effect; ChatGPT SMART ratings and an exploratory order-adjusted model did show significant effects. Findings depend on rater, outcome, model, and sequence.

updates.before: An applicant preparing a European Research Council Starting or Consolidator Grant proposal opens a chat session with a strong reasoning model, confirms that training on their data is turned off, and pastes in a published prompt that carries a condensed version of the current call's evaluation criteria, followed by their draft and its stage (pitch, synopsis with CV, or full proposal). The prompt tells the model to critique rather than write: it returns a plain-language summary, findings ranked by severity with each tied to a verbatim quote from the draft, structural score caps that fire when an expected element such as a risk plan is missing, what the next draft stage needs, and a paragraph to send to a human workshop reader. The applicant weighs each finding against the draft, pushes back on findings they disagree with on the merits, and revises the text themselves. Optional modules add a three-prompt sequence of panel reviewer, devil's advocate and writing coach, a mock-interview question bank, and an audit of a resubmission against a previous evaluation report. The package authors describe the tool as triage of routine structural problems so that mentors and workshops can concentrate on field-specific judgment, and say it does not replace human review. The output is a quoted, ranked critique that the applicant uses to plan revisions.

updates.before: Research-office staff and senior readers who run ERC grant workshops ask applicants, ahead of their session, to run their own draft through the published AI pre-review and bring three things: the draft, the AI critique, and up to three findings on which they want a human judgment. Workshop time then goes to what the package authors say only experienced readers can assess, such as whether the idea is at ERC level, panel strategy, field positioning and, later, interview credibility. Readers skim the plain-language summary first and, before forwarding it to a colleague, check that each of the top three summary sentences still matches the detailed finding it stands for. The applicant normally runs the tool; a reader may run it on someone else's draft only with the applicant's explicit consent, institutional approval and confirmation that training is off, keeping evidence of consent outside the tool. Where the AI critique and a human reader disagree on a high-severity finding, the human view prevails, and readers who serve as ERC panel members or remote referees never run the tool on proposals they are evaluating. The product is a focused workshop agenda built from the applicant's own selection of findings.

updates.before: A reviewer who has drafted a review for a conference or journal submits the review text and the paper to a multi-model feedback pipeline. Two models independently look for review comments that are vague or generic, questions already answered somewhere in the paper, and unprofessional remarks; an aggregator merges their lists, a critic removes inaccurate or nitpicky items, and a formatter pairs each flagged comment with suggested feedback addressed to the reviewer. Automated reliability tests screen the feedback before it is shown, rejecting items that merely praise the reviewer, address the paper's authors instead, restate the comment, or are malformed. The reviewer reads the suggestions and decides whether to revise; the system neither edits the review nor proposes new critiques. At ICLR 2025 the authors deployed it as a randomized trial on more than 20,000 reviews, reporting that about a quarter of reviewers who received feedback updated their reviews and that updated reviews were longer and rated more informative by blinded researchers. The authors publish the prompts and code for running the pipeline on one's own review.
updates.after: A reviewer who has drafted a review for a conference or journal submits the review text and the paper to a multi-model feedback pipeline. Two models independently look for review comments that are vague or generic, questions already answered somewhere in the paper, and unprofessional remarks; an aggregator merges their lists, a critic removes inaccurate or nitpicky items, and a formatter pairs each flagged comment with suggested feedback addressed to the reviewer. Automated reliability tests screen the feedback before it is shown, rejecting items that merely praise the reviewer, address the paper's authors instead, restate the comment, or are malformed. The reviewer reads the suggestions and decides whether to revise; the system neither edits the review nor proposes new critiques. At ICLR 2025 the authors randomized 44,831 reviews, selected 22,467 for feedback, and successfully delivered feedback to 18,946. They report that 26.6% of reviews receiving feedback were updated, and that updated reviews were longer and rated more informative by blinded researchers. The authors publish the prompts and code for running the pipeline on one's own review.
updates.reason: Use the detailed trial counts already reflected in the evidence field rather than repeating the abstract’s ambiguous more-than-20,000 phrasing.
